title: Reading Between the Lines
goals: Speculate about the present with must, can't, could, may and might (+ be / be + -ing).
Speculate about the past with must have, can't have and might have + past participle.
Tell apart -ed adjectives (how I feel) from -ing adjectives (what something is like), with their prepositions.
Talk about problems, accidents and achievements: get in trouble, get a scholarship, train for a marathon.
React with empathy and explain with You must be…, I see and You see.
Write impressions and opinions with My impression is that… and In my opinion, … about projects that improve lives.

learn.title: Speculating about the present: must, can't, could, may, might
learn.html:
When you don't know something for certain but you have clues, you make a guess. English uses modal verbs + base verb (or be + -ing for something happening now).

ModalCertaintyExample
must (not)Almost 100% sure (logical conclusion)She must be a genius. He must not sleep much.
can'tAlmost sure that it is impossibleThat can't be his sister; she's too old.
could / may / mightPossible, less sureHe could be a teacher. They might be feeling sad.
may not / might notMaybe notShe may not know the answer.
  • Structures: modal + be + adjective/noun (must be tired) and modal + be + verb-ing (must be working).
  • For the impossible we use can't, not mustn't: She can't be at home (= it is impossible that she is).
  • Modals do not take -s, do not take to, and do not use do/does in questions.

watch.why: Modals do not take -s in the third person.

watch.wrong: That mustn't be true. It's impossible!
watch.right: That can't be true. It's impossible!
watch.why: To say that something is impossible we use can't, not mustn't.
After the modal comes be + -ing, not a conjugated form.

learn.title: Speculating about the past: modal + have + past participle
learn.html:
To make guesses about something that already happened, use the same modal + have + past participle. It is a very useful extension at B2: it helps explain clues (a broken window, a friend who didn't arrive).

StructureMeaningExample
must have + participleSurely it happenedThe streets are wet. It must have rained.
can't / couldn't have + participleImpossible that it happenedShe can't have forgotten the meeting; I reminded her.
might / may / could have + participleMaybe it happenedHe might have missed the bus.
might not have + participleMaybe it didn't happenThey might not have heard the alarm.

With continuous actions in the past: They must have been waiting for hours. Remember: have does not change (not has) and it is pronounced weakly: «must've», «might've».

watch.wrong: She must has left her keys at home.
watch.right: She must have left her keys at home.
watch.why: After the modal it is always have, never has.

watch.wrong: He can't have being at the party.
watch.right: He can't have been at the party.
watch.why: The past participle of be is been.

watch.right: It must have rained last night.
watch.why: For the past, have + participle is missing.

watch.wrong: They must have went home early.
watch.right: They must have gone home early.
watch.why: After have we use the participle: gone, not went.

learn.title: -ed and -ing adjectives
learn.html:
Many emotion verbs have two adjectives. Those ending in -ed describe how a person feels; those ending in -ing describe what causes that emotion (a thing, a person, a situation).

-ed (how I feel)-ing (what something is like)
I'm bored with my job.My job is boring.
She's fascinated by astronomy.Astronomy is fascinating.
We were disappointed with the ending.The ending was disappointing.
He's frustrated with the traffic.The traffic is frustrating.
  • Common prepositions: interested in, excited about, pleased about, surprised by, bored with, annoyed with, scared of.
  • Some adjectives do not have an exact pair: scared (me) / scary (the thing); worried (me) / worrying (the situation).
  • A person can be -ing if they cause the emotion: He's boring = he bores other people; He's bored = he is bored.

watch.wrong: My sister is scary of spiders.
watch.right: My sister is scared of spiders.
watch.why: Scared of = to be afraid; scary = frightening.

learn.title: Giving impressions and opinions in writing
learn.html:
In a formal or semi-formal text (an email, a review, a comment) opinions are softened with introductory expressions. Almost all of them are followed by that + complete sentence (with subject and verb); in written language that can be omitted.

ExpressionExample
My impression is that…My impression is that you are passionate about the project.
It seems to me that…It seems to me that the program has helped many young people.
I think / believe / feel that…I believe that it is important to save cultural traditions.
In my opinion / view, …In my opinion, the rainforest is very valuable.

Watch out: In my opinion and In my view take a comma and don't take that. Say in my opinion; there is no word-for-word equivalent of «according to me».

watch.wrong: According to me, it's a great idea.
watch.right: In my opinion, it's a great idea.
watch.why: There is no literal English equivalent of 'according to me': use In my opinion.

watch.wrong: It seems to me what you worked very hard.
watch.right: It seems to me that you worked very hard.
watch.why: After It seems to me comes that, not what.

watch.wrong: In my opinion that the project is useful.
watch.right: In my opinion, the project is useful.
watch.why: In my opinion does not take that; it takes a comma.

learn.title: Reacting and explaining: must, I see, You see
learn.html:
• You must be… / That must be… — show that you understand the other person's situation or feelings: A: I just joined a band. B: That must be fun.
  • You see, … — explain something the other person may not know: You see, I used to practice every morning.
  • I see. — «ya entiendo» (you have just understood something new): A: The band keeps me motivated. B: I see.
  • It must be hard / stressful / exciting. — short empathetic reaction.
  • He can't be serious! — it can't be true, I'm surprised.
  • It could be…, but I'm not sure. — admit that it's only a guess.
  • Looking back, … / It turned out that… — it turned out that…, in the end.

write.prompt: Write an anecdote of 180 to 250 words about a time you drew wrong conclusions about someone or something (a neighbor, a coworker, a noise). Use at least three guesses with must / can't / might (present) and two with must have / can't have / might have (past), describe how you felt with -ed adjectives, and how the situation was with -ing adjectives. Close by saying what you learned.
targets: must / can't / could / may / might + be
prepositions with adjectives (interested in, scared of)
checklist: At least 3 guesses about the present with modal + be (+ -ing)
At least 2 guesses about the past with modal + have + participle
An ending with reflection (Looking back, it turned out that…)
No to and no -s after modals
write.model:
Last year I was sure that my new neighbor was a strange person. Every night, around eleven, I heard heavy noises coming from his apartment. He must be moving furniture, I thought. Then I heard voices. He can't be alone, I said to myself. He might be having a party, but nobody ever came in. I was quite worried, and I felt annoyed because I couldn't sleep.

First, I decided to ask my other neighbors. Then I noticed that he never smiled in the elevator. He must have had a bad experience, or he might have been angry with me. After that, I even thought he could have been dangerous, and I imagined that something terrible might be happening inside. I was interested in finding out the truth, but I was also scared of knocking on his door.

Finally, one evening I met him on the stairs. He was carrying a big drum. It turned out that he was a musician who practiced at night because he worked during the day. He felt embarrassed and apologized, and I felt ashamed for judging him. His music was actually fascinating, and the whole situation was a bit surprising.

Looking back, I learned that I can't know a person from the outside. He wasn't unfriendly; he was just shy. Now we are good friends.

At least 3 verbs or phrases from «Making a difference»
write.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to you because I recently read about your work with young people in my city, and I was very impressed. My impression is that your organization is making a real difference in the community, especially through the free workshops you offer after school.

It seems to me that programs like yours are essential. Many teenagers do not have a safe place to go, and they need adults who care about them and give them opportunities. In my opinion, education and support at this age can change a whole life. I also believe that your recycling project helps young people to protect the environment and to feel proud of their neighborhood.

I would like to offer my help as a volunteer. I am twenty-eight years old, and I work as a teacher, so I am used to working with teenagers. I am available on Saturday mornings and on some weekday evenings. I could help to run the workshops, raise money for the activities or take part in your cleanup days. I am also willing to donate some books and sports equipment to your center.

Please let me know if you need more information about me. I would be glad to come to a meeting and talk about how I can contribute.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Ricardo Mendoza

reading.title: The Mystery on Calle Morelos
reading.intro: Read the blog post and answer.
paragraphs: When Mrs. Aldana moved into the empty house at the end of our street, everyone in the neighborhood had a theory. My sister Paula was convinced that she must be a famous actress, because she arrived at midnight wearing dark glasses. My father said she couldn't be an actress; he thought she might be a retired judge, since she walks straight and rarely smiles.

I was fascinated, so I started to watch the house. Every morning at six, I heard a strange sound: long, slow notes followed by a short silence. It can't be a radio, I told myself, because the same notes kept repeating, as if someone were practicing. A week later, delivery trucks brought dozens of long black cases. Paula said they must contain equipment for a movie. I thought they might be instruments, but I didn't dare to say it.

One Saturday I felt too curious and knocked on her door. I was nervous and a little embarrassed, because I had no excuse. A tall woman with silver hair opened it. "You must be the boy who watches my windows," she said, smiling. I wanted to disappear. But she wasn't annoyed at all. "Come in," she said. "I think you've already guessed the secret."

Inside, the living room was full of violins, cellos and music stands. It turned out that Mrs. Aldana had been a conductor for thirty years in Vienna and in Mexico City. She had moved to our neighborhood to start a free program for children whose families can't pay for lessons. "The funding is small," she explained, "but music brings kids together. I've seen shy children overcome their fears just by playing in an orchestra. It's demanding work, but it's also very rewarding."

I left her house with a mix of feelings. I was surprised, because my sister's theory had been completely wrong, and I was excited, because I had always wanted to learn an instrument. Paula was disappointed that our neighbor wasn't a movie star, but she changed her mind when she heard the first rehearsal. "It's amazing," she whispered. "I never thought music could be so moving."

Now, six months later, thirty children practice in her living room every afternoon. I play the violin, though not very well yet. My father, the one who thought she was a judge, volunteers on Saturdays to carry the heavy cases. Looking back, I realize how easily we judge people from small clues. Our guesses were creative, but they were all wrong. Sometimes the best way to understand someone is simply to say hello.

tasks.model: Last year I gave a presentation at work. I was very nervous because the room was full of people. The beginning was frustrating, because the projector didn't work. But the end was amazing, and my boss said I did a great job. I was really proud of myself.

tasks.prompt: Talk about a person or organization you admire because they improve other people's lives. Give your impression and your opinion.
questions: Who or what organization do you admire?
What is your impression of their work?
Would you like to get involved?
tasks.model: I admire a local organization that teaches children to play music. My impression is that the teachers are very committed. In my opinion, music brings kids together and helps them overcome challenges. It seems to me that more people should support programs like this one, and I would love to volunteer.
